utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please call the case, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Sureta Chana, Philip Weiner, David Re, and Manoj Sachdeva for the Prosecution, very ably assisted by Ana Vrljic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's -- Peter Morrissey appearing with Guenael Mettraux and with legal assistant Amir Cengic and also assisted by Medina Delilac, present in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today it is the continuation of the Pre-Trial Conference. We will discuss some things in detail, especially concerning with the motions and the witness list. And before that, I would like to know whether the parties have received the draft guidelines sent informally by the Trial Chamber, and I would like to know at this stage are there any comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. We're grateful for receiving those guidelines. They are clear, and at this stage we have no comments to offer on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Likewise, Your Honour. We have no comments and we are also grateful for the guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that during the last Pre-Trial Conference as well as the Status Conference before, the Pre-Trial Judge instructed the parties should meet and discuss any agreement on matters of law as well as fact. If so, I would like to know are there any progress. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As to the question of facts, there is progress. We have had an exchange of facts. It's likely that a large number of background facts are to be agreed. We met yesterday for a number of hours. We don't have the list. We indicated the possibility of a report to the Court today. We can't comply with that, but what we can say is that there is material progress about facts, certainly background, uncontroversial facts. As to matters of law, I cannot give such an optimistic ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So there's still some differences between the parties concerning of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There remain such differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm a little bit surprised to hear that. Your letter -- there were no differences concerning of the matter of law rather than a lot of difference on the facts. Because the law is very clear and here in this case is not that, you know, complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it depends how specific Your Honour wants -- wants to be. We -- there are some matter where we want clarification from the Prosecution. These are not major matters. I must say they're small points that are being discussed between myself and Mr. Re and Ms. Chana as well, and it's safe to say there's likely to be progress about them. But we remain in discussion about the significance of some points of law. I thought I should raise that here in response to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the armed conflict, you know, is, you know, preconditioned to apply the law in this case, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with respect to that, we can indicate -- I know my learned friends have something to say about that. So do we. It's a matter that -- we submit that the Prosecution has to plead and that they should specify what the nature of the armed conflict is. The reason why they do is because of the need for -- in demonstrating the nexus, they will need to demonstrate what the link between the particular events are and the armed conflict in question. Those are the matters that should be pleaded. We are -- we may be in a position to make sensible concessions about it, and we may be in a position to do so today. But we would ask the Prosecutor to specify, do they say this is an international armed conflict or not. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that a relevant issue, the nature of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, may I turn to Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I confirm we did have some very meaningful discussions with the Defence counsel yesterday, myself and Mr. Re and Mr. Morrissey, and we have sort of pinned down -- we went through the indictment line by line, and Mr. Morrissey indicated his agreement or possible agreement to some of them, which -- pending him consulting his client. And in respect to the armed conflict, Your Honour, I don't think there's any relevance to the indictment as it stands now, whether there's an internal or an international armed conflict. And we did invite the Defence to tell us which armed conflict they would be agreeable to conceding. But as Mr. Morrissey has already indicated to Your Honours that he was going to, after consulting with his client, give a document of all the agreed facts. And also there's some documents, Your Honours, which we did agree the contents, at least some -- I think it was something like 12 documents, Your Honour, which the Court will not be burdened by because we have agreed on the contents of these overview documents. So pending Mr. Morrissey's now report, we will be able to file something with the Chamber hopefully by today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that I am quite encouraged by the progress made by both parties, and I am expecting a report by tomorrow. So I still hope that after this sitting, if both parties have time, you could sit together again and go over all those, you know, contents of the report as well as a short discussion concerning of matter of law. Thank you. It is so decided. The next issue is the witness list. The Trial Chamber has received the witness statements of all proposed witnesses, including the 92 bis statement. Here are still some questions I would like to ask the parties. The first question will go to the Prosecution: Did the Prosecution provide the statement of Mr. Mujezinovic to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can confirm that that statement has been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And did Defence receive all other statements it asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: With respect to the statements of Ms. Miletic and Mr. Husic, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position in respect of these two statements is we simply do not have them, and this is something we've already told the Defence and we cannot disclose what we do not have. As of now, from all our searches. As I said, these things do keep turning up. But from all due diligence searches, we simply do not have those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you going to call those two persons as a witness in your case?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are calling them as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you're going to call them and without any statement furnished to Defence, how could we proceed the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just clarify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I might clarify, Your Honour. We have received a statement in respect of Miletic and some statements in respect of Husic. But we -- but there are outstanding statements that are referred to in what we have. We are not bereft of material from those. We do have some. But there are statements referred to in their materials which make it manifest that there is another statement, at least, and that with respect to each. And that is what is currently missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that true, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we only have one statement from Miletic and -- which we have disclosed. We have no other statement. That is the position of the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe we could go through that statement and see what kind of statements requested by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: With respect to Miletic, Miletic says, "This is the second time I'm being interviewed" -- sorry, Your Honour, I'm paraphrasing here because I don't have the statement before me. But she indicates clearly that she's been interviewed by the ICTY investigators on another occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. We'll see to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond to that? And this is an issue which had been raised before the 65 ter Conference, where this very line was referred to by the Defence counsel. And our view on the matter is that sometimes the witnesses think they've -- when they talk to an investigator, they gave a statement. It's obviously a mistake on her part that she thinks that she's given another statement. That's what we surmise from that -- the first line of that statement of Miletic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. So in your view, there's no previous statement, interviews at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We have done all our searches, Your Honour, and we are not been able to identify any other statement from Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I make the observation about that. That Your Honour is in a difficult position in dealing with the materials here because obviously you can't search for them or involve yourself in it. All we can do on the Defence side is point to why we say there is a further statement, earnestly plead with the Prosecutor to look as hard as they can, and remind the Prosecutor that what Your Honour had just been told in respect to Ms. Miletic was in fact the Prosecutor's position about Mujezinovic and any such statement. But as it turned out, by looking hard, there was. And in good faith the Prosecutor then found that statement. It may be that by good fortune such a statement will be found, and we would like it because she's an early witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you are saying that, you know, once a thief, always a thief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the truth is that statements like that always return to those who make them. We don't suggest a thief in any way. What we suggest is that we -- we would like that statement because she's an early witness. And it may be a matter of some importance, so we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if -- if the Prosecution has shown good cause and -- and paid due diligence in this matter and exhausted all the efforts, still there's no statements available, so I think the Prosecution could be excused. Thank you. Here I have a request on the part of the Prosecution; that is, we hope that the Prosecution could furnish the Trial Chamber as well as the Defence with a list of the witnesses in the chronological order of their proposed appearances tomorrow, because we are going to hear the witness next Tuesday, so we should have a list at least for two weeks' witnesses. Is it possible, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We shall furnish that -- that list to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Briefly, we -- there's been a court order in the past indicating that the earlier witnesses to be called would be Grabovica witnesses, and we've structured our preparation accordingly so that in compiling the list of witnesses to be available, the Prosecution, in my submission, ought to bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can I get some confirmation from Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had indicated that we will endeavour to start with the Grabovica witnesses. And I think most of them are Grabovica witnesses at this time. And -- but there's been no sort of firm commitment that that's what we will do. That's our position, and we are trying to -- to start the -- the case in -- in that order, Your Honour. And I think the Defence will find that that's the order that it comes out in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's see your -- your list first. Yes. The next issue are the outstanding motions. The -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you go into that, I have another disclosure issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And of course I say this with a certain amount of embarrassment, Your Honour, having been -- what's just transpired. We do ask leave to disclose to Your Honours four statements; this is pursuant of the 7th May order imposed upon the Prosecution. Now, these are further statements we have discovered - and this is part of our due diligence searches, Your Honour - we have a statement from Selmo Cikotic, which was taken on 12th November 2004. We have a statement from Ahmed - how do you pronounce it? I'm sorry, I'm having difficulty with the pronunciation. Salihamidzic. It was taken on 6th November 2004. We have two statements from Jusuf Jasarevic, one which was taken on 29th November 2004 and another one taken on 28th March 2003. I'll come back to these statements, Your Honour, and explain the circumstances. And then there's one final one from Imam Zebic, taken on 6th November 2004. Your Honour, all of these -- first if I can explain the one from Jasarevic, which was taken on 28th March 2003. Your Honour, for that I can only humbly beg everyone's pardon. It was an oversight. And these statements do come out because, as I have indicated on many occasions - and I'm being repetitive here - we are doing searches. We do look at these searches. And they do throw up other statements which we had missed by all due diligence. Your Honour, this is a -- the nature of the beast, and I think this is something which all Trial Chambers and all Prosecution counsel face since our data banks are so huge. So as I said for that, I simply apologise. As for the others, the other statements, they were all taken in respect of another investigation that the Office of the Prosecution is conducting. And there is very little relevance other than I've had a look at the statements, other than one statement which has a slight relevance to this indictment. All the others are for a different crime base and another investigation. And they were taken in November 2004, and we just realised that they had not been disclosed. So in light of that, Your Honour, we are prepared to call these witnesses later in the day so that no prejudice is caused to the Defence in their preparation for the Defence. That is what we can offer to the Defence in light of our trespass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As a practice of this Tribunal, I believe that the disclosure should be completed six weeks before the start of the trial. The reason for that is to give the Defence enough time to prepare their case and to do some necessary investigations. I believe Mr. Morrissey has some good ideas on that. Could I hear your response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We agree with the general principle enunciated by Your Honour. The witnesses in respect of who these statements have been taken are each of them capable of being of great significance. The statement of Jusuf Jasarevic seems to be taken, if I heard correctly, on the 29th of November of 2004. And whilst of course I accept my learned friend's statement that there's an element of oversight in it, it's an astounding situation that a witness like that could have a statement taken at that time, which was overlooked by oversight, which would appear to be related to this case. And if that were an oversight, it's the sort of oversight that's really got to stop because it's embarrassing the Defence in their preparation. There are court orders in place ordering that disclosure cease, dated 15th of December, 2003 and 17th of December, 2004. As indicated on Monday, many times have the Prosecution been told to cease disclosure and many times have they undertaken to do so. And the question of good faith is not the issue here, and we don't seek in any way to impugn what my learned friend says. The question is: Can the Defence have any confidence and protection from the ongoing disclosure. I illustrate that by reference to Mr. Jasarevic who I've been personally preparing as a witness who was said to come quite early in the trial for three days. Now we have this material. Now, Your Honour, I raise this as an issue. We don't know what's in these statements. It would be premature now to say precisely how the Defence is prejudiced and indeed it's scientifically possible, though unlikely, that the Defence isn't prejudiced. We need to see what's in the statements, of course. But it places us in a position of embarrassment. Let me be clear that the Defence does not wish this matter postponed. Mr. Halilovic is now in custody, has been waiting for a long time, and the benefits usually brought about by postponements and adjournments now have to be weighed against the -- the detriments of such palliative measures. So, Your Honour, at this stage, all we can do is to agree sadly with Your Honour's comment that it's desirable that these matters be resolved earlier, note that we're likely to be prejudiced by what is being done, and ask the Prosecution to indicate why it is now that we shouldn't believe there are many more statements coming at arbitrary and unpredictable times and how we can prepare this case in anything like peace and order so that we don't waste the Tribunal's time, as I feel perhaps I am now making this speech. We'd rather be talking about something useful, but we're protesting against the disclosure practices that we have been complaining of for 12 months. When my learned friend asked to be liberated from the disclosure regime on Monday, the Court can readily see why they shouldn't be. They should be compelled to seek leave each time and to provide a detailed explanation each time as to why the material wasn't provided. Other than that, I wasn't told about this before I came to court, and I know nothing about it, Your Honour. But I can say that these witnesses are all capable of being significant witnesses, and this is significant material. And I'll close these comments by saying that apart from the statement of Mr. Jasarevic, statements relating to the other witnesses with respect to other investigations can remain of central relevance because the credit of at least two of those witnesses and, depending on the circumstances, all of them, may become an issue in this case. And therefore material going to their credit, particularly if they're being questioned about other war crimes - we don't know - is relevant and Rule 68 material that we should have and need. So there is nothing trivial on the face of it about the other four statements. As to Jasarevic, it looks bad, but I say no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very sorry to hear that there are so many oversights on the part of the Prosecution for their -- for their obligation to disclose the materials. We'll start the case next Monday, but still there's some materials or statements that need to be disclosed to the Defence. But at this stage, it's very difficult for the Judge to assess how the Defence is prejudiced against, unless we see the contents of those materials. So I believe that we will order that the Prosecution to disclose those materials to the Defence as well as to the Chamber as early as possible. Then - then - we'll consider how to deal with them after hearing the submissions from the parties. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we come to the outstanding motions. I see everybody nodding. The first motion we are going to deal with is a motion for striking out paragraphs in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. Up to now, we haven't heard any response from the Prosecution. I just want to know whether they want to respond to this motion or not. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Re will be dealing with this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour mean in the sense of respond orally today in court or to file a written response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you could do whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I can give you a response orally today. I gave you one in general terms on Monday. Our response is really no different to the response I gave on Monday. We view the motion as superfluous if not frivolous in the context of the proceedings here. The Defence is properly on notice of the case, and most of the matters referred to in that motion relate to the evidence which will be produced at trial by the Prosecution. And the Defence is well and truly on notice of that from the statements we have served on them and the exhibits and discussions we have had and our supplement setting out the case theory, which the Defence have. The Prosecution view is that such a motion should not really even be entertained by the Trial Chamber because it actually serves no purpose in the expeditious conduct of these proceedings. And we are quite frankly mystified as to why it has been filed and why it has been filed in the week before trial and the purpose of it, because even if the Trial Chamber were to grant the relief sought, which is to strike out certain portions of that document, it doesn't or wouldn't preclude the Prosecution from leading the evidence, which it has notified the Defence it intends to lead in pursuit of the allegations. The Prosecution maintains that its case is properly pleaded and the Defence have in accordance with the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, have proper notice of the material facts, the -- the allegations against their client, and all the evidence which we intend to lead against them in the coming weeks -- against the accused in the coming weeks. And at this late stage of the proceedings, this is an irrelevant diversion from the real matters which are sorting out the witnesses we can call, the exhibits we will tender, the order of exhibits, and the proper conduct of the trial. If Your Honour -- if Your Honour requires a written response to it -- I just don't want to waste the Court's time at this particular point. We could go on for a lot longer and respond to various things in it. If Your Honour wishes to -- wishes the Prosecution to file a written response, we will do so within the time accorded in the Rules, unless Your Honour truncates it. But that's -- that's the basic response to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we should reduce the paperwork as much as possible. Your position is quite clear, at least to me. I just want to hear a very concise rebuttal or response, whatever, in the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. I'll be as concise as I can in relation to this matter. My colleague from the Prosecution has indeed identified the two issues which are of some concern to the Defence, which is, one, the issue of notice; and, second, the evidence which is going to be led at trial. Concerning the first issue, the issue of notice. The position of the Defence is that the pre-trial brief may indeed provide some further particulars as to the facts which are being pleaded in the indictment. On the other hand --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. It is too fast for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and the concern of the Defence is that that is precisely what the Prosecution is attempting to do, in other words, trying to go beyond the indictment through the pre-trial brief. The other issue of concern to the Defence is that of the evidence which will be led by the Prosecution, and the concern that the Defence has is that some of that evidence will be evidence that goes to facts which are not properly or not sufficiently pleaded in the indictment. And the nature of our motion is to have those parts of the pre-trial brief which are nowhere to be found in the indictment stricken out of the Prosecution pre-trial brief so that the Defence is not faced at the end of the Prosecution case with a suggestion that it had adequate notice of those facts. Adequate notice of material facts must be found in the indictment and they are not. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Here I just want to stress one point, that the finding of this Trial Chamber will be based on the indictment, not on the pre-trial briefings. And the pre-trial briefings are just for reference purpose. And if we need to seek some clarifications on the point which is in the indictment, we might refer to the pre-trial briefs. And I want to stress that in no way the pre-trial brief could be served as evidence in this case and is just the positions and the case of one side. The Trial Chamber will consider the submissions from both parties and render its decision early next week. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There are two very short points that we would like to place on the record following the comments made on Monday by the Prosecution. The first one relates to the pre-trial brief. The record tends to suggest that the old pre-trial brief, which was filed on the 17th of June, 2002, still is a valid pre-trial brief, despite the fact that a new pre-trial brief of the Prosecution has been filed on the 13th of October, 2004. This is the Defence understanding that it is not so and that only the new pre-trial brief stand to this day. The second point which we would like to place on record: Consider the suggestion -- concern the suggestion which was made by the Prosecution that the material facts or pleading contained in their supplementary explanation of December of last year would in some way provide some degree of notice to the Defence of what their case is. This supplementary explanation was denied by the Trial Chamber on the basis that it was a non-permissible attempt to file an amendment to the pre-trial brief. The Defence consider it has received no notice about what the Prosecution case is in relation to that supplementary explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for drawing my attention to these two points. But I also have a question to ask you, Mr. Mettraux: That is, how about your pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As Your Honour will be aware, this pre-trial brief - and as my lead counsel underlined on Monday - was filed a long, long time ago by prior counsel. We were invited late last year by the previous Trial Chamber to file a new pre-trial brief. As we indicated in one of our filings, we were unfortunately not in a position, having neither the resources, not the time to file a new pre-trial brief at that stage, which in fact forced us to continue to stand by the one that was filed in 1993, June, if I'm -- if I'm correct. And this is the pre-trial brief of the Defence for the time being, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. I just want to know whether you agree with your -- you know, the -- the previous pre-trial brief or not. How about the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, there are matters which may require some explaining on the part of the Defence in relation to that pre-trial brief, to the extent that some of the statements made in that brief may not be sufficiently clear. And it is very possible that should we have the time to do so in the course of the Prosecution case orally before the beginning of our case, we should make those elements as clear as possible to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you mean that there's still a possibility for you to file a new pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wouldn't suggest that we would go as far as filing a new pre-trial brief. I don't think that we will have either the time to do that or that there would be a need for that. But there may indeed be some amendment in relation to some limited issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may intervene at this point. The Defence made a point that they were forced to -- to maintain their old pre-trial brief. I feel this deserves a comment, and I would like to place it on record that at the time this question of resources was never brought up. They simply stated that the old pre-trial brief stands. This is a new issue which counsel has raised today, and I would like the record to reflect that this was not the position at the time they were given the opportunity to respond to the pre-trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for reminding me of that point. Let's come to the next motion. The next motion is for the postponement of witness testimony and for full disclosure of the relevant materials. And since this motion concerning some particular persons -- and my suggestion is that we'll go to the private session. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in the open session. The next issue is about the Prosecution's application for leave to permit testimony via video conference link. We haven't received any response from the Defence yet. Mr. Morrissey, could you please just simply state your views on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, if the Court was -- if the Tribunal was minded to determine that matter now by oral -- after hearing oral argument, we would be content to present such argument. I can indicate that our position at the moment is that on the material provided, we would not be in a position to -- to consent to the -- to the order sought and to the motion, and we would oppose it on the material currently provided. That material falls short in a number of ways, and I can present argument if -- if you would wish to hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But we concede -- I'll make it clear, we concede there's a big public interest in the determining the matter quickly, that the Prosecution have a legitimate interest in that too. Very well. Well, Your Honour, the first issue about it is -- is this: That the Prosecutor has to establish a number of matters -- sorry, would Your Honour just excuse me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Sorry, Your Honour. My learned co-counsel has assisted me here. Your Honour, the four matters that have to be established in order for the Prosecutor to succeed in the application is, first of all, that the witness is unable or unwilling to come to the Tribunal. At the moment, it would appear simply that unwillingness has been established on the current material. Secondly, the testimony of the witness has to be shown to be sufficiently important to make it unfair to proceed without it. Now, that -- again, we'd submit that -- that the material you have falls short of that. It's just simply not spelled out why it is that this evidence is of such great significance. In that regard, it should be recalled that these witnesses are what might be described as "left bank witnesses." And it's the Prosecution's case that these killings took place on the right bank, by units established on the right bank and quartered or billeted on the right bank. Thirdly, it's got to be established that the accused wouldn't be prejudiced in the exercise of his right to confront the witness. These witnesses are -- it's not right for Defence counsel to cast dispersions on them when they're not here. But what I put here is that there is a tolerable likelihood that issues of credibility will be raised and that there may be challenges to aspects of their evidence, whether it be memory or truthfulness, we'll have to wait and see. But it can't be said these are witnesses who are uncontroversial witnesses. They give evidence as to timing, and they will be tested on their recollections directly upon that. And it therefore will be for the Court to form a view about them. And the Court is better able to form that view if you can see the witness. The accused is prejudiced by not seeing -- by not having the Court see those witnesses and assessing them. And that is a fundamental matter which doesn't need to be repeated many times but must -- but can't be forgotten. We'd submit that's the founding matter and that the status quo is that unless the Prosecution show that the other matters overwhelm that, that it is the interest. And Rule 71 bis provides that it is -- the moving party, the Prosecutor, has to establish if it's in the interests of justice to do this. Now, to come to the concrete case, you have two brief and, we submit, inadequate medical reports which have been advanced to indicate that these, both witnesses, are old and have each different health concerns. We do not dispute that they have those concerns. That material does not go so far as to suggest that the witnesses are unable to travel to The Hague or would be prejudiced or -- or that their health would be prejudiced by doing so and nor has it been pointed out why it is worse to go to The Hague than it is to go to Sarajevo. One can imagine that evidence could be led to that extent, if it existed. Such evidence would be easy to find if it existed and should be presented if it existed. And indeed, if it existed, the Defence may well take -- might, in some circumstances, take a different view. But you have to deal with it, Your Honour, on the basis of what you have. And that's why we -- and that's the way we have to deal with it too. And so that's why we take the -- the stance that we take. And in particular, we say that you have to draw a distinction between the inconvenience to a witness and genuine troubles which would allow an extraordinary measure to be taken, which in some cases is highly appropriate. But on the current material, which I stress - the current material - we say that the Prosecution has not established what it needs to for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A very short response. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Court knows, video conferencing is used in practically every case. It's used by Defence. It's used by Prosecution. Both sides have the opportunity to question a witness, test the witness, test their memory, test their credibility. In this case, these people are both two elderly women. Both have been sickly. We have medical reports from doctors in each case, both of them recommend that neither person attends. Both of these witnesses are important to the case. They talk about murders being committed. They talk about timing. They talk about -- one of them speaks of conversations with Croatian -- with soldiers who tell them that the Croatians in the village are to be killed, that she is to be executed. She identifies -- that's (redacted). She identifies the body of (redacted). The other also saw bodies, also is corroborative as to certain deaths. The government or the Prosecution has to establish that certain persons were killed. The timing of those killings, the perpetrators, and also on the issue of consciousness or guilt, that certain acts were taken to hide the bodies. And these witnesses explain each of those. As I stated, they're both elderly. They both would have -- find it difficult to come here. To go from -- from -- where they live in the middle part of Bosnia to Sarajevo is an hour and a half. To go from there and then to -- an hour and a half and a drive and then to get on an airplane and fly for another two to three hours where these people have brittle bones and they're -- and they suffer from certain physical conditions is too much to ask, and we'd request that the video conferencing be allowed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since this matter is an urgent issue and we might hear these two witnesses next week, so I believe that the Trial Chamber is in the position to make a ruling on this issue. We believe that those two witnesses are quite relevant to this case and their evidence might be -- have some probative value to this case. And we also believe that the ill health is found to be a sufficient reason to establishing that a witness is unable to come to the Tribunal to appear as a witness. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that the anticipated evidence of those two persons in relation to the Prosecution's case is sufficiently important to make it unfair to proceed without it. And the Trial Chamber is satisfied that sufficient reason has been shown to establish that the two witnesses are unable to come to the Tribunal. So the ruling is the Trial Chamber therefore decided that the testimony of those two witnesses should be heard by a video conference link. As for the specific time, we hope that the Prosecution should get in touch with the registrar as soon as possible to arrange the proper time and inform the Trial Chamber as well as the other party as soon as possible, since it is an urgent matter. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We'll make those notifications, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The next issue is about the Prosecution's application for leave to disclose Rule 66(A)(ii) material pursuant to the Trial Chamber's decision of May 7th, 2004. Under this filings also related to one particular witness, shall we go to the private session or we could do it in open session? I'm in your hands. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Perhaps we ought to go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No objections? Yes, I saw their nodding. So we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that the Trial Chamber has a general duty to ensure that the proceedings are not unduly delayed and that the accused has adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence. We believe that the Prosecution has to show the due diligence and good cause when requesting changes in its exhibit list at this stage of the proceedings. So there are some questions that I would like to put to the Prosecution, that is -- the first one is: Why so late? Why was the request for variation of the exhibit list not filed six weeks before the starting of the trial? Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the exhibit list was necessitated. We looked at it again after we had fine-tuned our witness list and we had withdrawn a lot of witnesses from our -- from our list and the motion is pending before Your Honours. And at the end of the day, Your Honour, we have added only 34 new witnesses and we have taken away 17 -- exhibits. I'm sorry, Your Honour. The other reason, Your Honour, is that some of these exhibits came from new collections which we had received late last year. And this is the ABiH collection, which is what we just referred to earlier on, that it all -- was all put onto the EDS suite. So these new materials necessitated some additional material to be put as exhibits onto an exhibit list, hence the delay for these additions, Your Honour. But we have compensated by taking some exhibits away. And as I indicated earlier, Your Honour, there will be some which we have agreed upon which, again, the Court will not be burdened with. And that is the explanation as to the lateness of the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I wonder whether those exhibits has already been furnished to the Defence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We have received them half an hour before this hearing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you are not in the position to give a thorough response for each exhibit at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Your Honour. In relation to the substance of those exhibits, we stand by our submissions of, I believe, the 24th of this month in relation to the admission of those exhibits. Insofar as their content is concerned, as we pointed out in our response, we haven't had the time and we haven't had time obviously to look into those new proposed exhibits at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But -- but the Prosecution believe that those exhibits will all have probative value and relevance, you know, to this case, I believe. Right, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree with you entirely in that respect. But the other thing I would like to point out is that the exhibit lists had been filed and the Defence have had all the exhibits for some time now. It is only the new additions, which I said which were some 34 documents which have been provided today. The rest of the documents, which were already on the exhibit list, the Defence have had them and they've had the documents themselves because we gave them hyperlinked. So it is only 34 documents, Your Honour, which we have disclosed physically today because we did it by motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, only 34 documents. So that is a big amount of documents. I don't know, you know, how thick each document is, but 34 documents is -- is a bundle of paper, you know, I must say. That will take some time, you know, for the Defence to -- to leaf through it, you know. So we are not in the position to -- to make any decisions at this stage, I believe that. I hope that the Defence could give their response concerning of those 34 documents as soon as possible, and at the same time we also hope to be furnished with those, you know, 34 documents so that we could be in a better position to make a decision as early as possible. Is that agreeable?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we shall undertake to do so, Your Honour. We are quite concerned, however, that we will have to divert some of our resources at this very, very late stage to do such a thing. And this is quite concerning to the Defence, all the more so that the Prosecution may attempt to tender some of those exhibits early in its case. And this is definitely something we would like to place on the record. If Your Honour orders us to file further submissions in relation to the substance of those exhibits, we shall definitely undertake to do so and as -- as soon as we can. As early perhaps as Monday or Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll see how relevant those documents are and how important, you know, they might be in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps a short comment in response to this. The problem the Defence is facing at this stage is that those documents are being put forth by the Prosecution as new exhibits without much information to the Defence as to how they may or are or are said to be relevant to the Prosecution case. It puts the Defence in the strange position of having to fight with a ghost in some sense and guessing what those documents are here for. I believe, with respect, that this would be a matter for the Prosecution to address and to convince the Chamber that indeed there is good cause, not only in relation to the very, very, very late disclosure of that material but also as to its relevance to this case and why some of those documents were not identified earlier. The Prosecution has told us about the majority of documents, which was found more than a year and a half ago, which is a long time, and also a minority of documents, which apparently have been found, identified by the Prosecution much before. The Defence would find itself in a very strange position of having to convince the -- the Prosecution perhaps, but the Trial Chamber in any case that those documents should not be admitted at this late stage without knowing exactly what they are for. We have seen the index to those documents, and from some of those documents we seem to -- to know what they are. But there are other documents which are totally new to us. And we will have to -- we would have to prepare for those and be ready potentially to cross-examine witnesses in relation to these documents, and it is indeed a very, very difficult situation for us to do so at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. A very good suggestion. Ms. Chana, would you please file a filing listing that -- why those documents were disclosed so late, whether you have been -- paid due diligence to this issue and whether there's any good cause to have those late disclosure at this time and how relevant those documents to each paragraph account in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution will file such a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope we could get that as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: How many days would you like it within, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Next Monday it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. The next issue is the urgent motion for immediate disclosure. I believe that almost all the issues in this motion has been dealt of -- dealt with, you know, in the previous discussions. If there's none, the Defence counsel might remind me of anything. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As Your Honour just pointed out, most of the issues in relation to that urgent motion of the Defence of 16 December 2004 have now been dealt with. There remain two, however, which require the Chamber attention. The first one relates to a witness referred to as Witness X. This witness, the Prosecution has now sought leave to withdraw this witness from its list of witnesses. The Defence still thinks and submits, however, that a finding of the Trial Chamber is still necessary in relation to the material going to that individual. First, the Defence has submitted and resubmits that this material is clearly Rule 68 material. The Defence has reserved its right to make further submissions pursuant to Rule 68 bis in relation to that matter. There is another aspect relating to the abuse of the process in relation to that motion, which is relevant. Finally, if the material is what the Defence believe it could be, is directly relevant to the credit or reliability of that witness or former witness, depending what the Trial Chamber decision is, it might as well be relevant to the credit and reliability of other related witnesses directly related to this one. The second issue, which is still pending before this Trial Chamber and which is of the utmost urgency for the Defence, is the material concerning the status as suspect of each and every Prosecution witness in this case, not only the witness we have been discussing before but each and every one of them. And I again refer the Trial Chamber to the order of November 2003 of the Trial Chamber in this case, which ordered the Prosecution to give that material a long, long time ago to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I still cannot understand how the credibility of a witness is related to the Rule 68. But that is a issue I might need some research on that, you know. But at this moment, I fail to see the relevance to the Rule 68. Maybe I'm wrong, but -- but I promise you I will do some research in this respect. As for, you know, other suspects, I doubt it very much whether the Defence need that, if those people are not called as a witness. Why should you need those, you know -- you know, features, their situations? I couldn't understand that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, if I haven't been totally clear on this matter. I think it's become quite clear to this Trial Chamber that the Defence has been suffering waves of late disclosure in this case. As a result of those successive waves of late disclosure, the Defence has been, we submit, greatly prejudiced. And the Defence intends to seek proper remedy either as a sanction to those violations or as a means of protection from further violations from the Prosecution. We believe at this stage that the finding from the Trial Chamber that the material in question was and is exculpatory and should have been disclosed months, if not years before, it's important to the Defence to make those submissions and to obtain an adequate remedy in relation to this matter. Concerning Your Honour's question -- unfortunately, I am going through my file -- but there is a decision of the ICTR Appeals Chamber in relation to the issue of criminal participation and credit of the witness which the Defence would be very happy to submit to the Trial Chamber in due course, if so requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. Yes, please. And I agree with the Defence that, you know, in this case the late disclosure on matters, you know, involving the disclosure cost the great inconvenience to the preparation of the case by the Defence. As for the degree and how the accused was prejudiced against, and I believe that the Trial Chamber needs an assessment on that issue. But here we are doing all our best first to start the case. Second, you know, to guarantee the legitimate rights of the accused. And thirdly, we hope we could do everything to make up what we lost and what is not insufficiently furnished before. We will see what we could do and we'll see, you know, how far we could go. And at this moment I could only say that I am looking forward to the cooperations from the both parties with good faith. The next issue is the Prosecution's motion to vary its list of -- of witnesses. I'm surprised that the Defence objects to withdrawal of eight witnesses. In other cases, you know, when the Prosecution proposed to withdraw some witnesses from their list, these suggestions is always welcomed by the Defence. But here we -- we see some objections from the Defence. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there's some witness who appear to be directly relevant and material witnesses to events that are controversial in the case. Now, the -- the keynote witnesses in that regard were Zicro Suljevic, S-u-l-j-e-v-i-c, and Rifat Bjelajac. They're both witnesses who are eyewitnesses to meetings which are said to found command responsibility. They're both people who were said to be members of the inspection team -- well, they both -- in fact, that's not -- they're not said to be. They were members of the inspection team, which inspection team is said to be the -- the location from which Halilovic became a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since -- since I don't know about protective measures for each witness, just please do not mention the names and they -- and just show me some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I will, Your Honour. Very well. Well, concisely speaking, two of the witnesses are people who were direct participants in the -- in the functions that Mr. Halilovic was carrying out, are directly relevant to his whereabouts at specific times, a matter which despite Your Honour's comment on Monday is not and, we think cannot be the subject of agreement with the Prosecutor right now. They are witness who can give evidence about where he was at particular times. There's one matter pleaded in the -- in the indictment which concerns the -- the gesture and the -- and the threat. Well, they're said to be there. They're said to be right there. How could they not be called by the Prosecutor? The indication given--

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just pardon me. Witnesses who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It was the position of the Prosecutor that these witnesses in particular were not to be called because they'd indicated that they didn't want to come. Now, there are obviously legitimate reasons why a Prosecutor will withdraw many witnesses and most of the witnesses - and there have been many that the Prosecution has withdrawn - we have no quarrel with. But those two are witnesses who are central. Their names are mentioned many times in footnotes to the original pre-trial brief. It will become apparent that the same applies with respect to the expert witness that the Prosecution have sought to rely upon. And in short, they were central to the indictment and to the earlier processes of this court, and we say should not be withdrawn. It's an unusual step for the Defence to submit that the Prosecution discretion be interfered with, but the Defence can be exposed by -- not necessarily deliberately so but to an unfair manipulation of the witness list. And sceptical accusers, of which I'm not one, might sometimes suggest that the Prosecution simply want [sic] to cross-examine a witness who is not convenient for them. We do not make the allegation here. We just simply say that they are both witnesses who should be called. Likewise, the presence of Mr. Halilovic being at issue -- there are other witnesses who are relevant to that question. Admissions or comments and accounts given by the accused man, Mr. Halilovic, whilst in custody are at issue in this case. And one of those who had him in custody is a relevant -- potentially relevant witness. Witnesses who are able to comment about the investigation, the timing of the investigation, and when the investigation was launched, people who can say things about when the news came in, when the police or authorities first became aware of what happened in Grabovica. Witnesses -- central witnesses in short. Central witnesses really ought to be called. And where the Prosecutor is making an allegation or is -- is withdrawing them for reasons which are manifest in respect of some of these witnesses, we say nothing. But these witnesses -- and in particular the two I mentioned initially -- were central to the indictment and they ought to be called. And so it's for those reasons that we take what, I frankly agree with Your Honour, is an unusual step in the unusual circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But generally speaking, you know, how the Prosecution to present its case and how many witnesses and whom to call is entirely within the discretion of the Prosecution or the party calling the witnesses. And if you believe that those, you know, witnesses are essential to this case, you may call them as your witness in your case in Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- with respect, that's always an appropriate response, and it's a matter that -- and there are various remedies to the Defence, including in some circumstances inviting the Chamber to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But with particular reference to the two that I mentioned and shouldn't have mentioned at the start of my submission, they are witnesses who were absolutely central, and a brief perusal of the Prosecution's original pre-trial brief will make it clear why -- how that is and why it is. The Prosecution have sought leave to vary the list, and it's implicit in that that leave is a matter that the Court grants and does not simply do it because the Prosecution asks and does so, acting judicially and considering all proper -- all the relevant matters. The Prosecution's discretion is an important one and is not likely to be interfered with, I concede. With respect to at least those two that I mentioned, they on their face - and we say on the face of material - constitute a special case, and one where the Prosecution ought to demonstrate good cause to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any response? Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is grateful for your observations at this regard, and we are completely in agreement with the observations you made that it is prosecutorial discretion as to how we submit the case and the witnesses we want to call. And if the Prosecution feel that some witnesses might be economical with the truth, we are quite within our rights not to call such a witness. Your Honour, there's no resume that I can -- that the Defence has referred to as to how the Prosecution can be forced to call certain witnesses. They are quite entitled to call any witness they want from the -- the witnesses that we have dropped from our witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But there are also seven new witnesses that you want to add into the witness list. We just want to know why you added those witnesses to the list at this late stage. Can you show us a good cause for doing that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you give me a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have added additional witnesses because we have cut out two-thirds of our witness list and we felt that there were some other witnesses which were necessary to prove the theory of our case. And these things are inevitable, as the Prosecution looks at their case and finds there are some other witnesses which may have probative value and enable the Chamber to establish the truth of the matter. And that is the reason why these particular witnesses have been added to the list. And I -- we, the Prosecution's position, is that notice has been given of this to the -- to the Defence. They have -- have had ample time to prepare for these new witnesses. And it is to assist the Trial Chamber in coming -- in determining the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please, very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very, very briefly. Just to point out the fact that every single one of those witnesses, I believe, although I have some reservation about the last one on the list, but in any case the five major witnesses have all been interviewed by the Prosecution in prior times. They were known to the Prosecution. The Prosecution had statements of those witnesses. And they were free to seek leave to add them to their list months, if not years ago. They've decided, for good reason or bad reasons, never to do so. We're now faced with another daunting task in addition to all the others which we've discussed before, of potentially preparing for yet new witnesses. The Prosecution also, for the record, has been claiming for months and probably for a year and a few months that they were ready for trial. Considering the making of such statements on repetitive occasions, the Defence finds it quite difficult to understand that a month before trial we should be faced with a new set of witnesses, new exhibits, a new pre-trial brief, and an attempt to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that this matter is quite an urgent matter, since we are going to have our first group of witnesses next week. So the Trial Chamber will consider the submissions from both parties and make a decision as early as possible early next week, you know, to fix that, you know, sliding sense or daunting target, you know, whatever, as the Defence phrased it. Well, I believe that's all, you know, for the motions at this moment. As for the last matter, that is, you know, we get in touch with the registrar and conveyed the views concerning of the seating arrangement raised by Defence the last time. The answer is that, you know, since it is the practice of this Trial Chamber which follows to almost every trial, so the seating arrangement should not be changed. And but we also are aware that the Defence counsel will have full freedom to get contact with his client even during the trial. So if there's something that the accused would like to inform their counsel, he could put it down on a piece of paper and ask a guard to pass to the Defence counsel and the Defence counsel, please feel free to approach your client during the proceedings. This is what we could do at this stage. I hope that will answer the request from Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that leave to approach is what I was going to ask for in the alternative. We're grateful for that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I hope that both parties could meet again after this sitting, and I'm expecting a report on the areas that parties has agreed upon as well as a witness list for the -- at least for the next week. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention to me? Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Very, very briefly once again. It's an issue that relates to the indictment. The Prosecution late last year filed what was known as a supplementary explanation to its pre-trial brief. As I pointed out earlier, this supplementary explanation was subsequently rejected by the Trial Chamber. Within that supplementary explanation, there is a suggestion that the notice or the alleged notice received by Mr. Halilovic took place on the 8th or 9th or September, 1993. The matter was raised again during the Rule 65 ter conference of 7 January, where the Defence pointed that issue and the contradiction between the tentative or attempt at amending the pre-trial brief by the Prosecution -- and the face on the indictment, which only mentioned the 8th of September 1993. The Senior Trial Attorney for Trial Chamber III at the time indicated to the Defence that the Defence was entitled to proceed upon the basis of the indictment, that is, upon the pleadings which are clear on their face, that such notice was -- was alleged to have been given on the 8th. The Prosecution in its supplementary explanation indicated that it may or may not decide to seek leave to amend the indictment. We've now been informed that the Prosecution would not seek such leave to amend the indictment. The Defence wants to make it very clear and to put it on the record that we do not consider having received any sort of notice on the part of the Prosecution that this new case, which is not pleaded in the indictment, is part of the Prosecution case, the supplementary explanation having been rejected and the Prosecution having decided not to seek leave to amend the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe this matter was mentioned during the last Status Conference presided by Judge Kwon, I suppose. Can I seek some confirmations on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The position is quite clear. Judge Kwon mentioned quite correctly that it's a matter of evidence. It's not a material particular of the indictment. We have made it very clear to the Defence that we will be calling conflicting evidence from different witnesses many years after the event as to whether or not he received notice on the 8th or the 9th. We are not in a position at this stage to elect at this stage whether it is the 8th or the 9th. We have foreshadowed that to the Defence. We did it last month, a good six weeks before trial in our attempt to file a supplementary explanation. The Defence have all the relevant statements. They know that some witnesses will say it was the 8th and some will say it was the 9th. This does not in any way prejudice the accused because the accused has been on notice for a long time of the conflict in the Prosecution statements. It's not a case where the date is a material particular of the pleading, such as in one where a crime is gazetted from a certain day or a statutory sexual assault charge where age is in issue or something like that. The position of the Defence clearly in their pre-trial brief, wherever -- whatever the status of that is at the moment, is that the accused, Mr. Halilovic, was not there and was not informed. So it doesn't matter from the perspective of the Defence preparation. The Prosecution foreshadowed that it may intend or may wish to amend the indictment to put in the words "8th" -- either "8th" or "9th." His Honour Judge Kwon made it clear that this was not necessary because at any time during the proceedings an indictment can be amended on such a matter. And at the end of the proceedings, the Trial Chamber can make a finding based upon the evidence, whether it was the 8th or the 9th. That's part 1. Part 2, in relation to the status of that supplementary explanation, the intended purpose of our filing that was simply to give the Defence good and adequate notice of the emphasis in the theory of our case. That is all. And to ensure that there was -- they had no prejudice in their preparation as to the emphasis of the theory of our case, based upon the pre-trial brief, the indictment, and everything which has been served on them. So that we say that the emphasis is on the failure to prevent and the use of the troops of the 9th and the 10th in Grabovica. The evidence has not changed. It's just that the submission the Prosecution will make, I anticipate, at the end of the proceedings may be slightly different. Now, whether or not the Defence chooses to take the view that they are not on notice because the Trial Chamber has said it is -- has -- has rejected the filing on the narrow basis that it was not a proper addendum with proper leave sought to the pre-trial brief is irrelevant. The Prosecution maintains the Defence is entirely and fully on notice from the day we served it of the way we intend to open the case and argue the case on exactly the same evidence, whether you call it a supplement, a letter of notification, or whatever you will. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Shortly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very briefly. Just to mention the exact quote from Judge Kwon at the latest -- the last Status Conference. And I quote his word: "The Defence is entitled to understand the nature of the case and whether you intend to amend the indictment. Could you do that in a week's time from today?" Clearly the indication was that if the Prosecution continues to be the one which was attempted in the supplementary explanation of December, they have an obligation. And the submissions of the Prosecution are quite incorrect. The Rules provide for the ways and methods in which you give adequate notice of material fact. The time of notice of an alleged crime and the alleged notice is a crucial material fact. And if indeed this is part of the Prosecution case, this can be pleaded in only one place, and it's the indictment. And if it is still the Prosecution case that this is part of its case, it can't be pleaded or mentioned simply in a supplementary brief which has been rejected or otherwise in the opening statement. It has to come through a motion to amend the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, no matter whatever Judge Kwon said and no matter whatever the positions held by both parties, I would like to say that in my view it is very difficult to fix a date on certain things which happened about ten years ago. So I regard this matter is a matter of the evidence, not a matter of the charge. It is so decided. Yes. Are there any other matters? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. There's just a housekeeping matter that sometimes troubles the Defence and may do so in this case. We have been assisted by the Registry and the CLSS interpreting and translating service and assisted greatly by them, but we still have a significant quantify of material outstanding which that service is attempting to deal with for us. When it creates a problem, we will let the Court know, but we don't want to complain on the morning and seem to have just invented a problem. So we mention that there's still, we think, something in the order of 30 per cent of documents that remain to be dealt with by them, and we can indicate that there's some outsourcing arrangements being sought, and we are trying to do what we can to deal with that. But should we apologise to the Court in the future and say that we -- we are short of a document, that may be one of the reasons and I mention it now. Without any criticism to the Registry, because they are doing absolutely everything they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. I believe that our trial will be in session from next week, so all the translations in this trial should be put on the list of priority. And if there's any problems concerning with the logistic issues as well as translation, please let us know as soon as possible. This Trial Chamber will do its best to help both parties, especially the Defence, to prepare their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for that indication. That will help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So next Monday we'll start with the opening statement by the Prosecution at 9.00. That opening statement will last two hours to two and a half hours. No objections is allowed as well as comments. If the Defence would like to make their opening statement at that time, they could do so, but in most of cases they will do that at a later stage, when they have a better picture of the Prosecution's case. Having said that, I declare the hearing is adjourned.
